argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Dialectical engagement with objections, using distinctions and thought experiments to defend a causal-historical theory of reference against descriptivist challenges.
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: Moderate: premises are often implicit in examples and distinctions, but key claims are stated directly.

argumentative_quality.dialectical_reasonableness: High: The text fairly presents both descriptivism and Kripke's alternative, and engages with Searle's objections in a nuanced way.
argumentative_quality.logical_relevance: All points are directly relevant to the question of whether baptism requires descriptive content.
argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: The premises rely on widely accepted intuitions about naming practices and thought experiments, though some are contestable.

distinctions_drawn: Descriptive content vs pragmatic role of demonstratives
Three senses of 'identify' (unique description, unique selection in context, causal encounter without re-identification)
De re vs de dicto intentions (implied)
explicit_definitions_given: Rigid designator: designates the same object in every possible world in which it exists.
Baptism: initial naming event that can involve demonstration, description, or causal contact.

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: The text anticipates and responds to several objections: (1) baptism requires descriptive content, (2) demonstratives have descriptive content, (3) uniqueness is needed, (4) intentions must have an object. Each is addressed with distinctions or counterexamples.
objections_raised: Searle: baptism must be guided by identifying intention, so descriptive content is necessary.
Searle: demonstrative 'this object' has descriptive content.
Searle: baptism must uniquely identify one object.
Searle: intention must have an object, so a descriptive intention is required.

epistemic_stance_and_voice.certainty_language_frequency: Moderate: uses phrases like 'may seem', 'can be', 'seems', but also asserts conclusions confidently.

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Thought experiments, conceptual distinctions, and analysis of ordinary naming practices.
named_thought_experiments: Naming a child (Lydia) while unable to distinguish from twin
Pointing to one of two objects
Naming a mountain seen briefly from a train

philosophical_orientation.grounding: Analytic philosophy, philosophy of language, reference theory.
philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Defends a causal-historical theory of reference against descriptivist objections, but acknowledges the role of descriptions in fixing reference in some cases.
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Proper names, reference, rigid designation, baptism, causal chains, descriptive content.

structural_organization.structure_type: Sectioned essay with introduction and numbered sections (I-IV). The text is incomplete, ending mid-sentence in section IV.

summary_of_core_decisions: The essay argues that Kripke's theory is not fundamentally descriptivist. It presents descriptivism, Kripke's alternative, Searle's challenge, and then a detailed response distinguishing three senses of 'identify' and epistemic vs metaphysical uniqueness. The central claim is that baptism does not require uniquely identifying descriptions; demonstrative, causal, and perceptual relations suffice. The text is cut off while discussing de re vs de dicto intentions.

thesis_commitment.conclusion_type: Defends a positive thesis: Kripke's theory is not descriptivist; Searle's objection fails.
thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low: The text is assertive, though incomplete.
